History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
42-year-old man developed shallow breathing, chest tightness, lip tingling, and blotchy rash within 15 min of a wasp sting while gardening; clinician advised immediate antihistamine and ambulance transport for suspected early anaphylaxis.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Acute breathing difficulty after wasp sting.  
• Timeline:  
  – 0 min: Stung by a wasp while gardening.  
  – ~15 min later (time of call): Shallow breaths, chest tightness, lip tingling, blotchy skin rash.  
• Progression: Symptoms ongoing; patient unsure if worsening.  
• Exacerbating factors: Triggered by sting; none reported otherwise.  
• Relieving measures: None taken prior to consult.  
• Associated symptoms: No throat closing sensation; denies prior similar episodes.  
• Review of systems (pertinent):  
  – Respiratory: Shallow breathing, chest tightness; denies wheeze (unable to auscultate remotely).  
  – Dermatologic: Blotchy rash; lip tingling without obvious swelling.  
  – ENT: No throat swelling/closure.  
  – Cardiovascular, GI, GU, neuro: Not discussed.  
• Pertinent negatives: No prior anaphylaxis; no asthma history.

Past Medical History:
• Eczema (details not provided).  
• Aerosinusitis when flying (managed with antihistamines).  
• Drug allergy: Penicillin → reported allergy (reaction details not specified).  
• Surgical history: None mentioned.  
• Other chronic illnesses: None reported.

Medications:
• Antihistamines (name/dose/route/frequency not documented); taken PRN for flying.  
• No regular daily medications reported.

Social History:
• Lives with wife; wife present at time of call.  
• Was gardening outdoors at onset.  
• Smoking: Not discussed.  
• Alcohol / recreational drugs: Not discussed.  
• Occupation / finances: Not discussed.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
(Remote video; no vitals or physical exam performed)  
• General appearance: Patient speaking in full sentences; reports shallow breathing.  
• No objective exam findings available.

Investigations:
• None performed during virtual visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Suspected early anaphylaxis / systemic allergic reaction to wasp sting  
  • Assessment: Sudden respiratory and cutaneous symptoms minutes after sting; high risk for progression to anaphylaxis.  
  • Plan:  
    – Advise immediate ambulance activation (wife to call 999).  
    – Administer available oral antihistamine now while awaiting EMS.  
    – Transport to Emergency Department for evaluation, potential epinephrine, airway management, observation.  
    – Educate patient and wife on urgency and potential for rapid deterioration.  

Issue 2 – Penicillin allergy  
  • Assessment: Documented medication allergy.  
  • Plan: Ensure allergy recorded in medical record; no further action today.  

Issue 3 – Chronic eczema / aerosinusitis  
  • Assessment: Stable; not contributory to current event.  
  • Plan: Routine care as needed; no acute management discussed.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Anaphylaxis secondary to wasp sting – High likelihood: Immediate multisystem (respiratory + cutaneous) symptoms post-sting; clinician’s urgent management plan supports.  
2. Systemic allergic urticaria without full anaphylaxis – Moderate likelihood: Rash and lip tingling present; respiratory symptoms may represent early progression.  
3. Anxiety/panic-induced hyperventilation – Low likelihood: Stressful event could cause dyspnea, but objective allergic rash favors allergic etiology.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Vital signs, full medication list, immunization status, smoking/alcohol history, detailed allergy reaction, ROS for other systems.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional minor gaps but clinically adequate.
